paragraphs: Friend, look at what Paul does with a crowd that wants him gone. He's in chains, he's just been dragged around, and he still asks, "May I say something to you?" (Acts 21:37). Then he stands on the steps and tells the story of what Jesus did in his life, starting with his own worst chapter (Acts 22:4). I'd have asked for a lawyer and a snack, and Paul asked for a microphone.

Here's the big idea: when Jesus changes you, your story is worth telling, even to people who aren't ready for it. Paul doesn't hide that he persecuted this Way "even to the death" (Acts 22:4). He tells it plainly, because the good part is who met him on that road: Jesus of Nazareth, who called him by name and gave him a job (Acts 22:8, 15). The crowd listened right up until the word Gentiles, then the shouting came back (Acts 22:21-22). Telling the truth about Jesus doesn't always get a warm reception, and Paul shows us that faithful is not the same as popular.

Now watch what happens in the barracks. Paul speaks up about his Roman citizenship and the soldiers step back at once (Acts 22:25-29). I think that's wisdom, not weakness, friend. He tells the truth when it's time to testify and uses what he's been given when it's time to be protected. Keep your story ready, baker, and keep your eyes open for the next door God opens.
